CHAPTER 28 - CONTEMPORARY PHYSICS

Introduction

Twentieth and twenty-first century physics reaches far beyond the classical world of Newton. Contemporary physics asks: What are the ultimate building blocks of matter? What forces hold them together? How can we probe them, and how can the same deep ideas be turned into technologies like the laser, the superconducting magnet, and engineered nanomaterials? This chapter surveys these frontier ideas at a conceptual level - the fundamental forces, elementary particles and the Standard Model, particle accelerators and detectors, lasers, superconductivity, nanotechnology, and the key ideas of the special theory of relativity. The emphasis throughout is on understanding, not heavy mathematics, though a couple of simple numericals (cyclotron frequency and E = mc^2) are worked out.

28.1 THE FUNDAMENTAL FORCES OF NATURE

Every interaction in the universe - a falling apple, a chemical bond, a decaying nucleus, the burning of the Sun - can be traced back to just FOUR fundamental forces:

(1) GRAVITATIONAL FORCE. Acts between any two masses. It is always attractive, has an INFINITE range, and follows an inverse-square law. Despite dominating the large-scale universe (planets, stars, galaxies), it is by far the WEAKEST of the four on the scale of particles.

(2) ELECTROMAGNETIC FORCE. Acts between electric charges (and magnets). It can be attractive or repulsive, has INFINITE range, and also obeys an inverse-square law. It binds electrons to nuclei to form atoms and binds atoms into molecules and solids - so essentially all of chemistry, light, electricity and magnetism is electromagnetic.

(3) WEAK NUCLEAR FORCE. Acts inside the nucleus over an extremely SHORT range (about 10^-18 m). It is responsible for certain radioactive decays, in particular beta decay, in which a neutron turns into a proton (or vice versa). It is much weaker than the strong and electromagnetic forces but stronger than gravity.

(4) STRONG NUCLEAR FORCE. Acts over a SHORT range (about 10^-15 m, the size of a nucleus). It is the STRONGEST of the four forces. It binds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus (overcoming the electromagnetic repulsion between protons) and, at a deeper level, binds quarks together inside protons and neutrons.

Relative strengths (taking the strong force as 1) are approximately: strong 1, electromagnetic 1/137 (about 10^-2), weak about 10^-6, gravitational about 10^-39. So gravity, though most familiar, is astonishingly feeble at the particle level; the strong force is roughly 10^39 times stronger. A useful summary:

  Force            Relative strength   Range        Acts on
  Strong           1                   ~10^-15 m    quarks, nucleons
  Electromagnetic  ~10^-2              infinite     charges
  Weak             ~10^-6              ~10^-18 m     quarks, leptons
  Gravitational    ~10^-39             infinite     all mass-energy

In modern physics each force is pictured as being carried by an exchange particle: the photon carries the electromagnetic force, gluons carry the strong force, the W and Z bosons carry the weak force, and the (still hypothetical) graviton would carry gravity. A long-standing goal of physics is UNIFICATION - showing that these forces are different aspects of one underlying interaction. The electromagnetic and weak forces have already been unified into the single 'electroweak' interaction.

28.2 ELEMENTARY PARTICLES AND THE STANDARD MODEL

The word 'elementary' means having no internal structure - a particle that is not made of anything smaller. Protons and neutrons were once thought elementary but are now known to be made of quarks. Particles are classified in two main ways.

By interaction and structure:
 - LEPTONS are truly elementary particles that do NOT feel the strong force. The best-known lepton is the ELECTRON. Others are the muon and the tau, together with three types of neutrino (electron-, muon- and tau-neutrino). There are six leptons in all.
 - HADRONS are particles that DO feel the strong force; they are made of quarks. Hadrons are subdivided into:
     * BARYONS - 'heavy' particles made of three quarks. Examples: the proton and the neutron.
     * MESONS - particles made of a quark and an antiquark. Examples: the pi-meson (pion) and the K-meson (kaon).

QUARKS are the elementary constituents of hadrons. There are six 'flavours': up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom. They carry FRACTIONAL electric charge - for example the up quark has charge +2/3 e and the down quark -1/3 e. A proton is made of two up quarks and one down quark (uud, total charge +1); a neutron is up-down-down (udd, total charge 0). Quarks are never found in isolation - they are permanently 'confined' inside hadrons by the strong force.

The STANDARD MODEL is the modern theory that organises all known elementary particles. It contains twelve matter particles (six quarks and six leptons), the force-carrier particles (photon, gluons, W and Z bosons) and the Higgs boson, which gives particles their mass. The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN in 2012, a triumph for the model. The Standard Model does not include gravity, so it is not a complete 'theory of everything'.

ANTIPARTICLES. Every particle has an ANTIPARTICLE with the same mass but opposite charge (and opposite in certain other properties). The antiparticle of the electron is the POSITRON (charge +e), predicted by Dirac in 1928 and discovered in 1932. When a particle meets its antiparticle they ANNIHILATE, converting their entire mass into energy (usually photons) according to E = mc^2. The reverse - pair production - creates a particle-antiparticle pair from energy.

28.3 PARTICLE ACCELERATORS AND DETECTORS

To study elementary particles we must give them very high energies and smash them together. This is the job of PARTICLE ACCELERATORS, which use electric fields to speed charged particles up and magnetic fields to steer them.

The CYCLOTRON, invented by E. O. Lawrence, is a classic accelerator. It has two hollow D-shaped electrodes ('dees') placed in a uniform magnetic field, with an alternating voltage across the gap. A charged particle moves in a semicircle inside a dee, gets a 'kick' of energy each time it crosses the gap, and spirals outward to higher and higher energy. The key result is that the frequency of revolution is INDEPENDENT of the particle's speed and radius:

   f = qB / (2 * pi * m)

where q and m are the particle's charge and mass and B is the magnetic field. This 'cyclotron frequency' is why a fixed-frequency alternating voltage can keep accelerating the particle. (Worked example below.)

Modern machines are SYNCHROTRONS - huge rings, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, 27 km in circumference - in which particles are steered around a fixed circle by ramping magnetic fields as their energy rises. DETECTORS surrounding the collision point record the tracks, energies and identities of the particles produced. Bubble chambers, cloud chambers, scintillation counters and modern silicon trackers are all detectors that make the invisible visible.

Worked example (cyclotron frequency): Find the cyclotron frequency of a proton (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg) in a magnetic field B = 1.0 T.
   f = qB / (2 * pi * m) = (1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.0) / (2 x 3.14 x 1.67 x 10^-27)
     = (1.6 x 10^-19) / (1.049 x 10^-26) = 1.53 x 10^7 Hz = 15.3 MHz (approx).

28.4 LASERS AND THEIR APPLICATIONS

LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. To understand it we need three ideas about how atoms interact with light:

 - ABSORPTION: an atom in a low energy level absorbs a photon and jumps to a higher level.
 - SPONTANEOUS EMISSION: an excited atom drops to a lower level on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction and phase (this is ordinary light, e.g. from a bulb).
 - STIMULATED EMISSION: a passing photon of exactly the right energy triggers an excited atom to drop, emitting a SECOND photon that is identical to the first - same energy, direction, phase and polarisation. Einstein predicted this in 1917. One photon becomes two, then four - light is amplified.

For stimulated emission to dominate, more atoms must be in the excited state than in the lower state - a situation called POPULATION INVERSION. This is not the normal thermal situation (where lower levels are more populated), so energy must be pumped in (optically or electrically) to achieve it. A laser consists of an active medium (which is pumped to population inversion) placed between two mirrors forming an optical cavity; one mirror is partly transparent to let the beam out.

PROPERTIES of laser light:
 - COHERENT: all the waves are in step (same phase).
 - MONOCHROMATIC: essentially a single wavelength / colour.
 - HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL: a very narrow, almost parallel beam that spreads very little.
 - INTENSE: energy is concentrated into a narrow beam.

APPLICATIONS of lasers: reading CDs/DVDs and barcodes; fibre-optic communication; laser printers; precise cutting, welding and drilling in industry; eye surgery (LASIK) and other medical uses; measuring distances (laser ranging to the Moon); holography; and research. These follow directly from the coherence, monochromaticity and directionality of the light.

28.5 SUPERCONDUCTIVITY AND NANOTECHNOLOGY

SUPERCONDUCTIVITY. In 1911 Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury cooled below about 4.2 K lost ALL electrical resistance - it became a SUPERCONDUCTOR. Below a material's CRITICAL TEMPERATURE (Tc) the resistance is exactly zero, so a current once started keeps flowing indefinitely with no energy loss. A second hallmark is the MEISSNER EFFECT: a superconductor expels magnetic field from its interior, so a magnet placed above it is levitated. 'High-temperature' superconductors (certain ceramic oxides) work above 77 K, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, making them cheaper to cool. Applications include powerful electromagnets for MRI scanners and particle accelerators, magnetically levitated (maglev) trains, and very sensitive magnetic-field detectors (SQUIDs).

NANOTECHNOLOGY. A nanometre is 10^-9 m; a NANOMATERIAL has at least one dimension in the range roughly 1-100 nm. At this scale, materials behave differently from their bulk form because a huge fraction of their atoms lie on the surface and because quantum effects become important. Gold nanoparticles, for example, appear red, not gold. Familiar nanostructures include CARBON NANOTUBES (rolled sheets of carbon, extraordinarily strong and good conductors) and GRAPHENE (a single layer of carbon atoms). Applications include stronger and lighter materials, faster electronics, targeted drug delivery in medicine, better solar cells, and improved catalysts. Nanotechnology is the deliberate design and use of such structures.

28.6 IDEAS OF THE SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY

In 1905 Albert Einstein published the SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY, built on two postulates:
 (1) The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.
 (2) The SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, is the SAME for every observer, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

The second postulate is deeply counter-intuitive and leads to remarkable consequences at speeds approaching c:

 - TIME DILATION: a moving clock runs SLOW as seen by a stationary observer. A fast-moving particle, or an astronaut in a fast rocket, ages more slowly. This is measured every day: fast-moving muons created in the upper atmosphere live long enough to reach the ground only because their 'clocks' run slow.
 - LENGTH CONTRACTION: a moving object appears SHORTENED along its direction of motion.
 - MASS-ENERGY EQUIVALENCE: mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, related by the famous equation

     E = mc^2

   A small mass is equivalent to an enormous energy because c^2 is so large. This is the principle behind the energy released in the Sun, in nuclear reactors and in nuclear weapons, and behind particle-antiparticle annihilation.

Worked example (E = mc^2): How much energy is equivalent to a mass of 1.0 gram?
   m = 1.0 g = 1.0 x 10^-3 kg, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
   E = mc^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3) x (3 x 10^8)^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3) x (9 x 10^16) = 9 x 10^13 J.
   That is 90 trillion joules from just one gram - enough to power a small town, illustrating why nuclear processes release so much energy.

At ordinary everyday speeds (far below c) these relativistic effects are utterly negligible, which is why Newtonian physics works so well in daily life. Relativity does not overturn Newton; it contains Newton as the low-speed limit.

SUMMARY

- Four fundamental forces govern all interactions: strong (strongest, short range), electromagnetic (infinite range), weak (short range, beta decay), and gravitational (weakest, infinite range). Relative strengths roughly 1 : 10^-2 : 10^-6 : 10^-39.
- Elementary particles: leptons (e.g. electron) feel no strong force; hadrons (baryons like the proton/neutron, and mesons) are made of quarks. Six quarks carry fractional charge and are confined.
- The Standard Model organises quarks, leptons, force carriers and the Higgs boson; every particle has an antiparticle (electron/positron); particle-antiparticle annihilation converts mass to energy.
- Accelerators (cyclotron, synchrotron/LHC) use electric and magnetic fields to give particles high energy; cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) is independent of speed. Detectors record the collisions.
- A laser produces coherent, monochromatic, directional, intense light by stimulated emission requiring population inversion; applications span communication, medicine, industry and research.
- Below its critical temperature a superconductor has zero resistance and expels magnetic field (Meissner effect); nanomaterials (1-100 nm, e.g. nanotubes, graphene) show new properties useful in medicine, electronics and materials.
- Special relativity (Einstein, 1905): the speed of light is constant for all observers; consequences include time dilation, length contraction and mass-energy equivalence E = mc^2.

glossary.definition: One of the four basic interactions of nature: gravitational, electromagnetic, weak nuclear or strong nuclear.
The strongest force; short range (~10^-15 m). Binds protons and neutrons in the nucleus and quarks inside them.
A short-range (~10^-18 m) force responsible for beta decay, in which a neutron changes into a proton or vice versa.
An elementary particle that does not feel the strong force, e.g. the electron, muon, tau and the neutrinos. There are six leptons.
A particle that feels the strong force and is made of quarks; hadrons are either baryons or mesons.
A hadron made of three quarks, such as the proton (uud) or the neutron (udd).
A hadron made of a quark and an antiquark, such as the pion or kaon.
An elementary constituent of hadrons carrying fractional charge (e.g. up +2/3 e, down -1/3 e). Six flavours exist; quarks are always confined.
The modern theory organising the elementary particles - six quarks, six leptons, the force carriers and the Higgs boson. It does not include gravity.
A partner of a particle with the same mass but opposite charge; the positron is the electron's antiparticle. A particle and its antiparticle annihilate into energy.
An accelerator using two dees in a magnetic field; the frequency of revolution f = qB/(2 pi m) is independent of the particle's speed.
The process in which a passing photon triggers an excited atom to emit a second, identical photon; the basis of laser action.
A condition in which more atoms occupy an excited state than a lower state, needed for laser amplification; achieved by pumping.
The complete disappearance of electrical resistance below a critical temperature Tc, accompanied by expulsion of magnetic field (the Meissner effect).
A material with at least one dimension of about 1-100 nm (10^-9 m), showing new properties, e.g. carbon nanotubes and graphene.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Contemporary Physics (NIOS Senior Secondary Physics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use c = 3 x 10^8 m/s where required. Show working for numerical problems. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Name the four fundamental forces of nature and arrange them in order of increasing strength.
questions.answer: The four fundamental forces are the GRAVITATIONAL, WEAK nuclear, ELECTROMAGNETIC and STRONG nuclear forces. In order of INCREASING strength: gravitational (weakest, ~10^-39) < weak (~10^-6) < electromagnetic (~10^-2) < strong (strongest, taken as 1).
questions.explanation: Relative strengths with the strong force set to 1.

questions.question: State any two properties of laser light and, for each, give one application that depends on it.
questions.answer: (1) MONOCHROMATIC (single wavelength) - used in fibre-optic communication and spectroscopy where a pure colour is needed. (2) HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL (narrow, near-parallel beam) - used in laser ranging (measuring distance to the Moon) and in precise cutting. (Coherence and high intensity are also acceptable, e.g. coherence for holography, intensity for welding.)
questions.explanation: Match a property to an application that relies on it.

questions.question: Explain how a laser produces light. In your answer describe stimulated emission and population inversion, and why population inversion is necessary.
questions.answer: LASER means Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Atoms can interact with light in three ways: absorption (an atom absorbs a photon and jumps up), spontaneous emission (an excited atom drops on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction and phase), and STIMULATED EMISSION - a passing photon of exactly the right energy triggers an excited atom to drop, emitting a SECOND photon identical to the first in energy, direction, phase and polarisation. One photon becomes two, two become four, and so on: the light is amplified. For stimulated emission to win over absorption, more atoms must be in the excited state than in the lower state - this is POPULATION INVERSION. In normal (thermal) conditions the lower state is more populated, so a photon is more likely to be absorbed than to cause emission; there would be no amplification. Energy is therefore pumped in (optically or electrically) to invert the populations. The active medium is placed between two mirrors (an optical cavity); photons bounce back and forth, stimulating more emission, and a partly transparent mirror lets the amplified, coherent beam escape. The result is coherent, monochromatic, directional, intense light.
questions.explanation: Cover the three atom-light processes, stimulated emission, and why inversion is essential.

questions.question: Distinguish between a baryon and a meson, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Both are HADRONS (they feel the strong force and are made of quarks). A BARYON is made of THREE quarks - example: the proton (uud) or the neutron (udd). A MESON is made of a quark and an ANTIQUARK - example: the pi-meson (pion) or K-meson (kaon).
questions.explanation: Baryon = 3 quarks; meson = quark + antiquark.

questions.question: What is the Meissner effect? State one application of superconductors.
questions.answer: The MEISSNER EFFECT is the expulsion of magnetic field from the interior of a material when it becomes superconducting (cooled below its critical temperature). Because the field is pushed out, a magnet can be levitated above a superconductor. One application: powerful superconducting electromagnets in MRI scanners (or maglev trains, or particle accelerators).
questions.explanation: Field expulsion below Tc; any valid superconductor application.

questions.question: A proton (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg) moves in a cyclotron with magnetic field B = 0.5 T. (a) Write the formula for cyclotron frequency. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) State why this frequency does not depend on the proton's speed.
questions.answer:
(a) Cyclotron frequency f = qB / (2 * pi * m).
(b) f = (1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.5) / (2 x 3.14 x 1.67 x 10^-27)
     = (8.0 x 10^-20) / (1.049 x 10^-26)
     = 7.6 x 10^6 Hz = 7.6 MHz (approx).
(c) As the proton speeds up, the radius of its circular path grows in exact proportion to its speed, so the TIME for one revolution stays the same. The speed cancels out of the formula, leaving f dependent only on q, B and m. This is why a fixed-frequency alternating voltage keeps the proton in step and accelerates it.
questions.explanation: Apply f = qB/(2 pi m); speed cancels because radius grows with speed.

questions.question: Calculate the energy equivalent of a mass of 2.0 g using E = mc^2 (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s).
questions.answer:
m = 2.0 g = 2.0 x 10^-3 kg.
E = mc^2 = (2.0 x 10^-3) x (3 x 10^8)^2
         = (2.0 x 10^-3) x (9 x 10^16)
         = 1.8 x 10^14 J.
So 2 g of matter is equivalent to 1.8 x 10^14 joules - an enormous energy, because c^2 is very large.
questions.explanation: Substitute into E = mc^2; note c^2 = 9 x 10^16.

questions.question: What is meant by time dilation? Give one real observation that supports it.
questions.answer: TIME DILATION means a moving clock runs SLOW as seen by a stationary observer; the faster the motion (approaching the speed of light), the greater the effect. A real supporting observation: muons created high in the atmosphere are short-lived, yet because they travel near the speed of light their 'clocks' run slow, so many survive long enough to reach the ground - far more than Newtonian physics would allow.
questions.explanation: Moving clocks run slow; atmospheric muons are the standard evidence.

questions.question: What is a nanomaterial? Give two examples and state why nanomaterials behave differently from bulk matter.
questions.answer: A NANOMATERIAL has at least one dimension in the range about 1-100 nm (1 nm = 10^-9 m). Examples: CARBON NANOTUBES and GRAPHENE (also gold nanoparticles, quantum dots). They behave differently from bulk matter because a very large fraction of their atoms lie on the surface and because quantum effects become important at this scale, changing optical, electrical and mechanical properties (e.g. gold nanoparticles look red, not gold).
questions.explanation: Size 1-100 nm; surface fraction and quantum effects cause new behaviour.

questions.question: What is an antiparticle? What happens when a particle meets its antiparticle?
questions.answer: An ANTIPARTICLE has the SAME MASS as its particle but OPPOSITE charge (and opposite in certain other properties). For example, the antiparticle of the electron is the POSITRON (charge +e). When a particle meets its antiparticle they ANNIHILATE: their entire mass is converted into energy, usually as photons, obeying E = mc^2.
questions.explanation: Same mass, opposite charge; annihilation converts mass to energy.

questions.question: List the four fundamental forces of nature.
questions.answer: The four fundamental forces are: (1) the STRONG nuclear force, (2) the ELECTROMAGNETIC force, (3) the WEAK nuclear force, and (4) the GRAVITATIONAL force.
questions.explanation: Simple recall of the four forces.

questions.question: Compare the strong and gravitational forces in terms of strength and range.
questions.answer: The STRONG force is the strongest of all four (relative strength 1) but acts only over a very short range, about 10^-15 m (the size of a nucleus). The GRAVITATIONAL force is by far the weakest (relative strength ~10^-39) but has INFINITE range and is always attractive. So gravity dominates the large-scale universe despite being feeble at the particle level, while the strong force dominates inside the nucleus.
questions.explanation: Contrast strength and range; note why each dominates in its domain.

questions.question: Why is gravity important on the astronomical scale even though it is the weakest force?
questions.answer: Gravity is always ATTRACTIVE and has INFINITE range, and it acts on all mass-energy. Large bodies like planets and stars are electrically neutral, so the much stronger electromagnetic force cancels out, leaving gravity to accumulate over huge masses and distances. That is why gravity governs planets, stars and galaxies.
questions.explanation: Infinite range + always attractive + acts on all mass, and EM cancels for neutral bodies.

questions.question: Distinguish between leptons and hadrons, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: LEPTONS are elementary particles that do NOT feel the strong force - example: the electron (others are the muon, tau and the neutrinos). HADRONS are particles that DO feel the strong force and are made of quarks - example: the proton (a baryon) or the pion (a meson).
questions.explanation: Key difference: strong-force interaction and quark content.

questions.question: What are quarks? State two of their key properties.
questions.answer: Quarks are the elementary constituents of hadrons (baryons and mesons). Key properties: (1) they carry FRACTIONAL electric charge (e.g. up quark +2/3 e, down quark -1/3 e); (2) they are permanently CONFINED - never found alone, always bound inside hadrons by the strong force. There are six flavours: up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom.
questions.explanation: Fractional charge and confinement; six flavours.

questions.question: Give the quark composition of a proton and a neutron.
questions.answer: Proton = two up quarks and one down quark (uud), total charge +1. Neutron = one up quark and two down quarks (udd), total charge 0.
questions.explanation: uud for proton, udd for neutron.

questions.question: What is the Standard Model? What does it not include?
questions.answer: The STANDARD MODEL is the modern theory that organises all known elementary particles: six quarks, six leptons, the force-carrier particles (photon, gluons, W and Z bosons) and the Higgs boson (which gives particles mass, found in 2012). It successfully describes the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions. However, it does NOT include GRAVITY, so it is not a complete 'theory of everything'.
questions.explanation: List contents; note that gravity is missing.

questions.question: What is an antiparticle? Give an example.
questions.answer: An ANTIPARTICLE has the same mass as its particle but the OPPOSITE charge (and opposite in certain other properties). Example: the antiparticle of the electron is the POSITRON, which has charge +e.
questions.explanation: Same mass, opposite charge; electron-positron.

questions.question: Describe what happens in particle-antiparticle annihilation and the reverse process.
questions.answer: In ANNIHILATION, a particle meets its antiparticle (e.g. electron + positron) and their entire mass is converted into energy, usually appearing as photons, obeying E = mc^2. The REVERSE process is PAIR PRODUCTION, in which sufficiently energetic radiation (energy) is converted into a particle-antiparticle pair. Both illustrate the equivalence of mass and energy.
questions.explanation: Mass to energy (annihilation) and energy to mass (pair production).

questions.question: Explain the working principle of a cyclotron.
questions.answer: A cyclotron has two hollow D-shaped electrodes (dees) in a uniform magnetic field, with an alternating voltage across the gap between them. The magnetic field bends a charged particle into a circular path inside a dee; each time the particle crosses the gap, the electric field gives it an energy 'kick'. As its energy rises, the particle spirals outward to larger radii, gaining energy at every crossing, until it is extracted at high energy. The revolution frequency f = qB/(2 pi m) is constant, so a fixed-frequency voltage keeps the particle in step.
questions.explanation: Dees + magnetic field for circular motion + electric field for energy; constant frequency.

questions.question: Calculate the cyclotron frequency of a proton (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg) in a field B = 1.0 T.
questions.explanation: Substitute into f = qB/(2 pi m).

questions.question: Why is the cyclotron frequency independent of the particle's speed?
questions.answer: As the particle gains speed, the radius of its circular path increases in exact proportion to the speed (r = mv/qB). The particle therefore travels a longer path at a higher speed, and the TIME for one revolution stays the same. Speed cancels out of f = qB/(2 pi m), so the frequency depends only on q, B and m.
questions.explanation: Radius grows with speed, so the period (and frequency) is unchanged.

questions.question: Explain stimulated emission and why it is central to laser action.
questions.answer: In STIMULATED EMISSION, a photon of exactly the right energy passes an excited atom and triggers it to drop to a lower level, emitting a SECOND photon that is identical to the first - same energy, direction, phase and polarisation. So one photon becomes two, the two become four, and so on: the light is AMPLIFIED. This multiplication of identical photons is what produces the coherent, monochromatic, directional beam of a laser, which is why stimulated emission is central to laser action.
questions.explanation: Triggered identical photon leads to amplification and coherence.

questions.question: State the four main properties of laser light.
questions.answer: Laser light is (1) COHERENT (all waves in phase), (2) MONOCHROMATIC (a single wavelength/colour), (3) HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL (a narrow, near-parallel beam), and (4) INTENSE (energy concentrated into a narrow beam).
questions.explanation: The four standard properties.

questions.question: What is population inversion and why is it needed for a laser?
questions.answer: POPULATION INVERSION is the condition in which MORE atoms are in an excited state than in the lower state. It is needed because only then does stimulated emission dominate over absorption, so that an incoming photon produces a net gain of photons (amplification) rather than being absorbed. It is achieved by pumping energy into the medium (optically or electrically).
questions.explanation: More atoms excited than in the lower state, so emission beats absorption.

questions.question: Give three applications of lasers and, for each, state which property is being used.
questions.answer: (1) Fibre-optic COMMUNICATION - uses the coherent, monochromatic beam that carries information with little distortion. (2) Laser CUTTING/WELDING - uses the intense, focused beam to deliver concentrated heat. (3) EYE SURGERY (LASIK) - uses the precise, highly directional beam to reshape tissue accurately. (Others: barcode reading and holography.)
questions.explanation: Match each application to the enabling property.

questions.question: Describe the two main properties of a superconductor and give one application.
questions.answer: (1) ZERO RESISTANCE: below its critical temperature Tc the electrical resistance drops to exactly zero, so a current flows without any energy loss. (2) MEISSNER EFFECT: the superconductor expels magnetic field from its interior, allowing a magnet to be levitated above it. Application: powerful superconducting electromagnets in MRI scanners (also maglev trains and particle accelerators).
questions.explanation: Zero resistance and Meissner effect, plus one use.

questions.question: Why are 'high-temperature' superconductors useful even though they still need cooling?
questions.answer: High-temperature superconductors (certain ceramic oxides) become superconducting above 77 K, the boiling point of liquid NITROGEN. Liquid nitrogen is cheap and easy to handle compared with liquid helium (needed for old low-Tc superconductors), so cooling is far less expensive and more practical.
questions.explanation: They can be cooled with inexpensive liquid nitrogen rather than liquid helium.

questions.question: Give two examples of nanomaterials and one application of nanotechnology.
questions.answer: Examples of nanomaterials: CARBON NANOTUBES and GRAPHENE (also gold nanoparticles, quantum dots). Application: targeted drug delivery in medicine (also stronger/lighter materials, faster electronics, better solar cells or catalysts).
questions.explanation: Two named nanomaterials plus a genuine application.

questions.question: State the two postulates of the special theory of relativity.
questions.answer: (1) The laws of physics are the SAME in all inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference. (2) The SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s) is the same for every observer, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
questions.explanation: The two postulates.

questions.question: Calculate the energy equivalent of a mass of 5.0 g (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s).
questions.explanation: Apply E = mc^2 with c^2 = 9 x 10^16.

questions.question: What is time dilation? Give one piece of evidence for it.
questions.answer: TIME DILATION is the slowing of a moving clock as seen by a stationary observer; the effect grows as the speed approaches that of light. Evidence: fast-moving muons produced in the upper atmosphere reach the ground in far greater numbers than their short lifetime would allow, because their internal 'clocks' run slow due to their near-light speed.
questions.explanation: Moving clocks run slow; atmospheric muons are the standard evidence.

questions.question: Describe the four fundamental forces of nature, comparing their relative strengths, ranges and the particles on which they act.
questions.answer:
There are four fundamental forces:
1. STRONG NUCLEAR FORCE - the strongest (relative strength 1). Short range, about 10^-15 m (nuclear size). It binds protons and neutrons in the nucleus and quarks inside them; carried by gluons.
2. ELECTROMAGNETIC FORCE - relative strength about 10^-2 (1/137). INFINITE range, inverse-square law, attractive or repulsive. It acts on electric charges, binding electrons to nuclei and atoms into molecules; carried by the photon.
3. WEAK NUCLEAR FORCE - relative strength about 10^-6. Very short range, about 10^-18 m. It causes beta decay (a neutron turning into a proton or vice versa); carried by the W and Z bosons.
4. GRAVITATIONAL FORCE - the weakest (relative strength about 10^-39). INFINITE range, inverse-square, always attractive, acts on all mass-energy; would be carried by the (hypothetical) graviton.
So strengths run roughly 1 : 10^-2 : 10^-6 : 10^-39 for strong : EM : weak : gravity. The short-range forces act only within nuclei; the infinite-range forces (EM and gravity) shape the everyday and astronomical worlds. Physicists have unified the electromagnetic and weak forces into a single 'electroweak' force, and seek to unify the others.
questions.explanation: Full comparison of the four forces with strengths, ranges, carriers and roles.

questions.question: Explain how elementary particles are classified. Describe leptons, hadrons (baryons and mesons), quarks and the Standard Model.
questions.answer:
Particles are classified by whether they feel the STRONG force and by their structure.
LEPTONS are truly elementary particles that do NOT feel the strong force. The electron is the best known; the others are the muon, the tau and three neutrinos - six leptons in all.
HADRONS DO feel the strong force and are made of quarks. They split into:
 - BARYONS: made of THREE quarks (e.g. the proton uud and the neutron udd).
 - MESONS: made of a quark and an ANTIQUARK (e.g. the pion and the kaon).
QUARKS are the elementary building blocks of hadrons. There are six flavours (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom) carrying FRACTIONAL charge (up +2/3 e, down -1/3 e). Quarks are permanently CONFINED - never seen alone.
The STANDARD MODEL organises all of this: six quarks, six leptons, the force carriers (photon, gluons, W and Z bosons) and the Higgs boson, which gives particles mass and was discovered in 2012. The Standard Model describes the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions very successfully but does not include gravity, so it is not a complete theory of everything.
questions.explanation: Systematic classification and the Standard Model overview.

questions.question: Explain the principle and construction of a cyclotron. Derive/state its frequency and calculate it for a proton in a 0.8 T field (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg).
questions.answer:
CONSTRUCTION: A cyclotron has two hollow D-shaped metal electrodes ('dees') placed in a strong uniform magnetic field, with a high-frequency alternating voltage applied across the gap between them. A charged particle is injected near the centre.
PRINCIPLE: Inside a dee (a field-free region) the magnetic field bends the particle into a semicircle. Each time it crosses the gap, the alternating electric field gives it an energy kick, increasing its speed. A faster particle moves in a larger semicircle, so it spirals outward, gaining energy at every gap crossing, until it is extracted at high energy.
FREQUENCY: For circular motion the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv^2/r, so r = mv/(qB). The time for one full revolution is T = 2 pi r/v = 2 pi m/(qB), which is independent of v and r. Hence the cyclotron frequency is
   f = 1/T = qB/(2 pi m).
CALCULATION (B = 0.8 T):
   f = (1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.8) / (2 x 3.14 x 1.67 x 10^-27)
     = (1.28 x 10^-19) / (1.049 x 10^-26)
     = 1.22 x 10^7 Hz = 12.2 MHz (approx).
Because f is fixed, a constant-frequency accelerating voltage keeps the proton in step throughout.
questions.explanation: Construction, principle, derivation of f = qB/(2 pi m), and a worked value.

questions.question: Explain the principle of a laser, including absorption, spontaneous emission, stimulated emission and population inversion, and list the properties of laser light.
questions.answer:
An atom can interact with light in three ways:
 - ABSORPTION: an atom in a low level absorbs a photon and jumps to a higher level.
 - SPONTANEOUS EMISSION: an excited atom drops on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction and phase (ordinary light).
 - STIMULATED EMISSION: a passing photon of the right energy triggers an excited atom to drop, emitting a SECOND photon identical to the first (same energy, direction, phase, polarisation).
LASER (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) uses stimulated emission to multiply identical photons. For this to dominate over absorption, more atoms must be in the excited state than the lower state - POPULATION INVERSION - achieved by pumping energy in (optically or electrically). The active medium sits between two mirrors (an optical cavity); photons bounce back and forth stimulating more emission, and a partly transparent mirror lets the beam out.
PROPERTIES of the resulting light: COHERENT (in phase), MONOCHROMATIC (single wavelength), HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL (narrow beam), and INTENSE. These properties underlie applications in communication, medicine, industry, data storage and research.
questions.explanation: Three processes, inversion, cavity, and the properties.

questions.question: Discuss four applications of lasers and, in each case, explain which property of laser light is essential.
questions.answer:
(1) FIBRE-OPTIC COMMUNICATION: relies on the MONOCHROMATIC and COHERENT beam, which can be modulated to carry data over long distances with little distortion or loss.
(2) MEDICAL SURGERY (e.g. LASIK eye surgery, cutting tissue): relies on the HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL beam that can be focused to a tiny, precise spot, and on its INTENSITY to cut or seal tissue cleanly.
(3) INDUSTRIAL CUTTING AND WELDING: relies on the high INTENSITY of a focused beam, delivering concentrated heat exactly where needed.
(4) HOLOGRAPHY (3-D images): relies on COHERENCE, since only in-phase light can record the interference pattern that stores three-dimensional information.
(Other examples: barcode/CD reading and laser ranging use the narrow, directional beam.) In each case the special property of laser light - coherence, monochromaticity, directionality or intensity - is what makes the application possible.
questions.explanation: Four applications each tied to the enabling property.

questions.question: Write short notes on (a) superconductivity and (b) nanotechnology, including key properties and applications of each.
questions.answer:
(a) SUPERCONDUCTIVITY: Discovered by Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911, it is the complete disappearance of electrical resistance when a material is cooled below its CRITICAL TEMPERATURE (Tc). Two hallmarks: (i) ZERO resistance - a current once started flows indefinitely with no loss; (ii) the MEISSNER EFFECT - the material expels magnetic field from its interior, so a magnet is levitated above it. 'High-temperature' superconductors work above 77 K and can be cooled with cheap liquid nitrogen. Applications: powerful electromagnets in MRI scanners and particle accelerators, magnetically levitated (maglev) trains, and ultra-sensitive magnetic detectors (SQUIDs).
(b) NANOTECHNOLOGY: the design and use of materials with a dimension of about 1-100 nm (1 nm = 10^-9 m). At this scale a large fraction of atoms lie on the surface and quantum effects matter, so properties differ from the bulk (e.g. gold nanoparticles look red). Important nanomaterials include CARBON NANOTUBES (very strong, good conductors) and GRAPHENE (a single carbon layer). Applications: stronger and lighter materials, faster electronics, targeted drug delivery, better solar cells and catalysts.
questions.explanation: Two structured notes with properties and applications.

questions.question: State the postulates of the special theory of relativity and explain its three main consequences, including a numerical illustration of E = mc^2.
questions.answer:
Einstein's SPECIAL THEORY OF RELATIVITY (1905) rests on two postulates:
(1) The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) frames.
(2) The speed of light in vacuum, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, is the same for all observers, independent of the motion of source or observer.
Three main consequences at speeds near c:
 - TIME DILATION: a moving clock runs slow as seen by a stationary observer (evidenced by long-lived fast muons reaching the ground).
 - LENGTH CONTRACTION: a moving object is shortened along its direction of motion.
 - MASS-ENERGY EQUIVALENCE: mass and energy are interchangeable, E = mc^2.
Numerical illustration: the energy equivalent of 1.0 g of matter is
   E = mc^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3 kg)(3 x 10^8 m/s)^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3)(9 x 10^16) = 9 x 10^13 J.
This huge figure from a tiny mass explains why nuclear reactions (in the Sun, reactors and bombs) and particle-antiparticle annihilation release so much energy. At everyday speeds (far below c) these effects are negligible, so Newtonian physics remains an excellent approximation.
questions.explanation: Postulates, three consequences, and a worked E = mc^2 value.

questions.question: What is an antiparticle? Explain particle-antiparticle annihilation and pair production, and state their connection with E = mc^2.
questions.answer:
An ANTIPARTICLE is the partner of a particle with the SAME MASS but OPPOSITE electric charge (and opposite in certain other quantum properties). Its existence was predicted by Dirac in 1928; the first one found was the POSITRON (the electron's antiparticle, charge +e), discovered in 1932. Every particle has an antiparticle.
ANNIHILATION: when a particle meets its antiparticle (for example an electron and a positron), the pair disappears and their ENTIRE MASS is converted into energy, usually released as photons (gamma rays). The energy released equals E = mc^2 (using the total mass of the pair), so annihilation is a direct demonstration of mass-energy equivalence.
PAIR PRODUCTION is the reverse: a sufficiently energetic photon (energy at least equal to the mass-energy of the pair) can be converted into a particle-antiparticle pair. Again the bookkeeping is governed by E = mc^2 - energy becomes mass.
Thus antiparticles show, in the clearest possible way, that mass and energy are interconvertible: matter can turn wholly into energy and energy wholly into matter.
questions.explanation: Definition, annihilation, pair production, and the E = mc^2 link.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

All interactions in nature can be traced to four fundamental forces. Taking the strong force as strength 1, the electromagnetic force is about 10^-2, the weak force about 10^-6, and gravity about 10^-39. The strong and weak forces are short-range; the electromagnetic and gravitational forces have infinite range.

(i) Which force is the strongest and which is the weakest?
(ii) Which two forces have infinite range?
(iii) Which force is responsible for beta decay?
(iv) Which force holds the nucleus together despite proton-proton repulsion?
questions.answer:
(i) Strongest: the STRONG nuclear force (strength 1). Weakest: GRAVITY (about 10^-39).
(ii) The ELECTROMAGNETIC and GRAVITATIONAL forces have infinite range.
(iii) The WEAK nuclear force is responsible for beta decay.
(iv) The STRONG nuclear force holds the nucleus together, overcoming the electromagnetic repulsion between protons.
questions.explanation: Direct reading of strengths, ranges and roles of the four forces.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Hadrons feel the strong force and are made of quarks. Baryons contain three quarks; mesons contain a quark and an antiquark. A proton is uud and a neutron is udd. Up quarks carry +2/3 e and down quarks -1/3 e.

(i) Are protons and neutrons baryons or mesons? Why?
(ii) Show that the charge of the proton (uud) is +1.
(iii) Show that the charge of the neutron (udd) is 0.
(iv) Name one particle that is NOT a hadron.
questions.answer:
(i) They are BARYONS, because each is made of THREE quarks (proton uud, neutron udd).
(ii) Proton uud: (+2/3) + (+2/3) + (-1/3) = +3/3 = +1. Charge +1 e.
(iii) Neutron udd: (+2/3) + (-1/3) + (-1/3) = 0. Charge 0.
(iv) The electron (a lepton) is not a hadron. (Any lepton or the photon is acceptable.)
questions.explanation: Apply quark charges to get proton and neutron charges; identify a non-hadron.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron. When a particle meets its antiparticle they annihilate, converting their mass into energy according to E = mc^2. The reverse is pair production.

(i) What is the charge of a positron?
(ii) Do a particle and its antiparticle have the same or different mass?
(iii) What is produced when an electron and positron annihilate?
(iv) Name the reverse process.
questions.answer:
(i) The positron has charge +e (opposite to the electron's -e).
(ii) The SAME mass.
(iii) Their mass is converted into ENERGY, usually appearing as photons (gamma rays).
(iv) The reverse process is PAIR PRODUCTION (energy converting into a particle-antiparticle pair).
questions.explanation: Antiparticle properties and annihilation/pair production.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a cyclotron, a charged particle moves in a magnetic field between two dees, gaining energy at each gap crossing. The cyclotron frequency is f = qB/(2 pi m) and is independent of the particle's speed. Consider a proton with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg in a field B = 1.0 T.

(i) Write the formula for the cyclotron frequency.
(ii) Calculate f for the proton.
(iii) What happens to f if B is doubled?
(iv) Why is f independent of the proton's speed?
questions.answer:
(i) f = qB/(2 pi m).
(ii) f = (1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.0)/(2 x 3.14 x 1.67 x 10^-27) = (1.6 x 10^-19)/(1.049 x 10^-26) = 1.53 x 10^7 Hz = 15.3 MHz (approx).
(iii) f doubles, because f is directly proportional to B.
(iv) As the proton speeds up, its orbital radius grows in proportion, so the time per revolution is unchanged; speed cancels out of the formula.
questions.explanation: Apply f = qB/(2 pi m); note proportionality to B and speed-independence.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In stimulated emission, a passing photon triggers an excited atom to emit a second identical photon. For this to amplify light, more atoms must be excited than in the lower state (population inversion). The resulting laser light is coherent, monochromatic, directional and intense.

(i) What does the word LASER stand for?
(ii) In stimulated emission, how does the second photon compare with the first?
(iii) What is population inversion?
(iv) List two properties of laser light.
questions.answer:
(i) Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
(ii) The second photon is IDENTICAL to the first - same energy, direction, phase and polarisation.
(iii) Population inversion is the condition in which MORE atoms are in the excited state than in the lower state, needed so that emission dominates over absorption.
(iv) Any two of: coherent, monochromatic, highly directional, intense.
questions.explanation: Definitions of stimulated emission, inversion and laser-light properties.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Lasers are used in fibre-optic communication, in industrial cutting and welding, in eye surgery, in barcode readers, and in holography. Each use depends on one or more special properties of laser light: coherence, monochromaticity, directionality and intensity.

(i) Which property is essential for holography?
(ii) Why is a laser suitable for precise eye surgery?
(iii) Which property lets a laser cut and weld metal?
(iv) Give one everyday device that uses a laser to read information.
questions.answer:
(i) COHERENCE is essential for holography (only in-phase light records the interference pattern).
(ii) Because the beam is HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL and can be focused to a tiny, precise spot, allowing accurate reshaping of tissue.
(iii) Its high INTENSITY (a focused, concentrated beam of energy) lets it cut and weld metal.
(iv) A CD/DVD player or a barcode scanner (or a laser printer).
questions.explanation: Match applications to enabling properties.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Below its critical temperature Tc, a superconductor has exactly zero electrical resistance and expels magnetic field from its interior (the Meissner effect). Superconducting magnets are used in MRI scanners and maglev trains. High-temperature superconductors work above 77 K, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.

(i) What is the resistance of a superconductor below Tc?
(ii) Name the effect by which a superconductor expels magnetic field.
(iii) Give one application of superconductors.
(iv) Why are high-temperature superconductors more convenient to use?
questions.answer:
(i) Exactly ZERO.
(ii) The MEISSNER EFFECT.
(iii) Superconducting magnets in MRI scanners (or maglev trains, or particle accelerators; SQUID detectors).
(iv) They can be cooled with cheap, easily handled liquid NITROGEN (boils at 77 K) instead of expensive liquid helium.
questions.explanation: Zero resistance, Meissner effect, applications, and the liquid-nitrogen advantage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A nanomaterial has at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nm (1 nm = 10^-9 m). At this scale a large fraction of the atoms lie on the surface and quantum effects become important, so properties differ from the bulk. Carbon nanotubes are very strong and conduct well; graphene is a single sheet of carbon atoms.

(i) What size range defines a nanomaterial?
(ii) Why do nanomaterials behave differently from bulk matter?
(iii) Name two nanomaterials mentioned in the passage.
(iv) State one application of nanotechnology.
questions.answer:
(i) About 1-100 nm (with 1 nm = 10^-9 m) in at least one dimension.
(ii) Because a large fraction of their atoms are on the surface and quantum effects become important at this scale, changing optical, electrical and mechanical properties.
(iii) Carbon nanotubes and graphene.
(iv) Any one: targeted drug delivery, stronger/lighter materials, faster electronics, better solar cells or catalysts.
questions.explanation: Nanoscale definition, cause of new behaviour, examples and an application.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Einstein's special relativity (1905) assumes the speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s is the same for all observers. Consequences include time dilation, length contraction and mass-energy equivalence E = mc^2.

(i) State the postulate about the speed of light.
(ii) What does time dilation mean?
(iii) Calculate the energy equivalent of 1.0 g of matter.
(iv) Why are relativistic effects unnoticed in daily life?
questions.answer:
(i) The speed of light in vacuum is the SAME for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
(ii) A moving clock runs SLOW as seen by a stationary observer (the effect grows near the speed of light).
(iii) E = mc^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3 kg)(3 x 10^8)^2 = (1.0 x 10^-3)(9 x 10^16) = 9 x 10^13 J.
(iv) Because everyday speeds are far smaller than the speed of light, so time dilation, length contraction and other relativistic effects are negligibly small.
questions.explanation: Postulate, time dilation, an E = mc^2 calculation, and why effects are hidden at low speed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The equation E = mc^2 says mass and energy are equivalent. Because c^2 is very large (9 x 10^16), even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous energy. This underlies the Sun's energy, nuclear reactors, and particle-antiparticle annihilation.

(i) What does E = mc^2 express?
(ii) Why does a small mass give such a large energy?
(iii) Calculate the energy from 0.5 kg of mass fully converted.
(iv) Give one real process that releases energy this way.
questions.answer:
(i) It expresses the EQUIVALENCE of mass and energy - mass can be converted into energy and vice versa.
(ii) Because the conversion factor c^2 is enormous (about 9 x 10^16 m^2/s^2), so multiplying even a small mass by c^2 gives a huge energy.
(iii) E = mc^2 = 0.5 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 0.5 x 9 x 10^16 = 4.5 x 10^16 J.
(iv) Any one: nuclear fusion in the Sun, a nuclear reactor/fission, or electron-positron annihilation.
questions.explanation: Meaning of E = mc^2, role of c^2, a calculation, and a real energy-releasing process.
